| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["272c86c6db95f1ef8b83f672b65e64df16494cae261e1aba1aeb1e59dcb68524", "defe25e400d4925d8a2bb4b1181044d06a8bf61688fd9c9ea59f1e0bb7bc21d8", "edc1f7528ca93ec432daca820f47e08d218b79cceca1ee764966f8f90d6a58bd", "ba86b6e0199b8907427364246f049efd67dc4eda0b5078f4bc7607253634cf24", "aea13e5871b683a19a05015ff0369b412b985d47eb67a3af93f44400a026b4b0", "b53069a380a9dd3dc1c758888d0e50dd43935f16df0f7124c77569375a9f44f5", "33580073680016f23bf474e6e62c61bf6a776e561385bfb06788a4713114ba9d", "498961237cf1c48f1e7764829818c5ba0af24a234c2f29c4420fb80276aec676", "4f4567abe9ff520797b04b04255bbbe07ecdddb594559d436ac53314ec62c1b3", "53f1b841d323c211c715b8f80d0efb9529440caae921a60340de027052946dd9", "bf94f4056627907d86ce1cae8b44c67a", "a2c6e01001c62f6198e31a9d603977c6", "d2a6009587b3cb73355c2d1e53d5cdfa"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-31431", "CVE-2026-43284", "CVE-2026-43500", "CVE-2024-21182", "CVE-2026-0257", "CVE-2026-45659")

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has

| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-31431", "CVE-2026-43284", "CVE-2026-43500", "CVE-2024-21182", "CVE-2026-0257", "CVE-2026-45659")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Identifies endpoints reporting Chrome installations vulnerable to CVE-2026-11645 and the four prior actively-exploited Chrome zero-days disclosed in 2026 (CVE-2026-2441/-3909/-3910/-5281). Joins to inventory to surface the actual installed version operators need to drive patch enforcement.

[LLM] Chrome process executing with pre-fix V8 version (149.0.7827.<102) post-disclosure Exploitation Medium
Detects chrome.exe processes whose runtime ProductVersion is below the fixed build (149.0.7827.102 Linux / .102-.103 Win+Mac) after the 2026-06-09 disclosure. Catches the residual-risk window where Chrome auto-updated the on-disk binary but the user has not yet relaunched — the running process is still vulnerable to in-the-wild CVE-2026-11645 exploitation. Rationale: Uses the exact patched-version threshold the article specifies (149.0.7827.102 Linux / .102-.103 Windows+macOS). Different telemetry source from UC1 — process-runtime ProductVersion rather than vuln-mgmt snapshot — so it catches the gap between 'binary updated on disk' and 'user actually relaunched browser', which is where in-the-wild exploitation of disclosed zero-days actually lands in real environments.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\mspub.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\visio.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:

      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.

New NFCShare Android Malware Delivered via Weaponized Versions of Egitimate Banking Apps

Cyber Security News
2026-06-09 2 use cases 0 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

A newly evolved strain of Android malware known as NFCShare is being spread through fake versions of legitimate banking apps, putting mobile users across Europe at serious risk. The malware is designed to secretly steal payment card data using a phone&#8217;s NFC chip, and it has grown into a much broader and more coordinated campaign [&#8230;] The post New NFCShare Android Malware Delivered via Weaponized Versions of Egitimate Banking Apps appeared first on Cyber Security News .

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Medium

French govt messaging service breached in account hijacking attack

BleepingComputer
2026-06-09 5 use cases 1 technique 5 kill-chain phases detected

DINUM, the digital affairs directorate of the French government, warned that hackers used a hijacked user account to breach Tchap, the French government's encrypted messaging platform. [...]

ATT&CKT1059.001
Domainsmatrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr tchap.gouv.fr

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] PowerShell script containing hardcoded LDAP bind with plaintext password (Tchap-leak vector)
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Mass /_matrix/media/ bulk download from tchap.gouv.fr to a single endpoint (Tchap exfil) · [LLM] High-rate Matrix client API enumeration against tchap.gouv.fr (room/user/media scraping)
[LLM] Mass /_matrix/media/ bulk download from tchap.gouv.fr to a single endpoint (Tchap exfil) Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the 13.5GB exfiltration vector from the June 2026 Tchap breach: a single client pulling large volumes of media via the unauthenticated /_matrix/media/r0/download/ endpoint across one or more *.tchap.gouv.fr shards. Tuned to fire when an endpoint requests media at rates or total bytes that exceed normal Tchap client behaviour. Rationale: Pivots on the article's two hard IOCs (`tchap.gouv.fr`, `matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr`) plus the attacker's own confession: 'Every file ever shared on Tchap, on any shard, is downloadable without a token. The media IDs come from the messages.' The cross-shard count is the article-specific differentiator — a normal civil servant client only talks to its own homeserver shard, so >2 distinct *.tchap.gouv.fr shards from one client is the signature of the token-less media-scrape behaviour the actor described.
ATT&CKT1530 T1213.003 T1567
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "tchap.gouv.fr"
| where RemoteUrl has "/_matrix/media/" and RemoteUrl has "download"
| extend Shard = tostring(parse_url(RemoteUrl).Host)
| summarize Downloads = count(),
            DistinctMedia = dcount(RemoteUrl),
            ShardsTouched = dcount(Shard),
            ShardList = make_set(Shard, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where Downloads > 100 or ShardsTouched > 2  // 100 = empirical Tchap-client baseline ceiling; >2 shards from one client is anomalous (1 user = 1 shard normally)
| order by Downloads desc
let TchapShards = dynamic(["tchap.gouv.fr", "matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any (TchapShards) or DstHostname has "tchap.gouv.fr"
| where Url has "/_matrix/media/" and Url has "download"
| extend Shard = tostring(parse_url(Url).Host)
| summarize Downloads = count(),
            DistinctMedia = dcount(Url),
            ShardsTouched = dcount(Shard),
            TotalBytes = sum(HttpResponseBodyBytes),
            ShardList = make_set(Shard, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)

| order by TotalBytes desc

[LLM] PowerShell script containing hardcoded LDAP bind with plaintext password (Tchap-leak vector) Weaponization High
Hunts for the exact artefact class the Tchap actor harvested: PowerShell scripts that embed `New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectoryEntry` / `LDAP://` bind strings alongside plaintext password assignments. Designed for proactive discovery so credentials can be rotated before they leak via chat — and for retrospective hunting on endpoints whose users have Tchap clients installed. Rationale: Built straight from the article's credential-leak claim: 'hardcoded LDAP credentials allegedly leaked via a PowerShell script shared by a French tax authority regional director.' The dual regex — LDAP bind primitive AND a `password=` literal in the same command-line / script body — is what distinguishes a credential-bearing script from a benign AD-query script. Hunting tier because the goal is proactive discovery of these artefacts on civil-servant endpoints before they get pasted into Tchap, not real-time alerting.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1213
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
// Hunt PowerShell processes whose command-line carries an LDAP bind AND a plaintext-password literal
let LdapPatterns = pack_array("DirectoryEntry", "LDAP://", "System.DirectoryServices", "ADSI", "DirectorySearcher");
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (LdapPatterns)
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(password|pwd|secret|userpassword|pass)\s*[:=]\s*[\"'][^\"'\s]{4,}"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountDomain,
          ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ProcessCommandLine,
          FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Cross-pivot: same script in DeviceFileEvents writes — likely the shareable .ps1 the actor exfiltrated
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName endswith ".ps1"
    | project FileTimestamp = Timestamp, DeviceName, ScriptFile = FileName, ScriptPath = FolderPath, ScriptSHA = SHA256
  ) on DeviceName
let LdapPatterns = dynamic(["DirectoryEntry", "LDAP://", "System.DirectoryServices", "ADSI", "DirectorySearcher"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any (LdapPatterns)
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(password|pwd|secret|userpassword|pass)\s*[:=]\s*[\"'][^\"'\s]{4,}"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| union (
    Event
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell" and EventID in (4103, 4104)
    | extend Script = tostring(EventData)
    | where Script has_any (LdapPatterns)
    | where Script matches regex @"(?i)(password|pwd|secret|userpassword|pass)\s*[:=]\s*[\"'][^\"'\s]{4,}"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Script
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PowerShell with hardcoded LDAP bind and plaintext password

status: experimental
description: Detects PowerShell processes whose command line contains an LDAP bind string and a plaintext password literal — the credential-exposure pattern leaked via chat in the June 2026 Tchap breach.
references:

detection:

[LLM] High-rate Matrix client API enumeration against tchap.gouv.fr (room/user/media scraping) Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the discovery + collection behaviour the actor used to scrape ~73,000 accounts and ~650,000 messages from a single hijacked Tchap account: bursty calls to /_matrix/client/r0/sync, /joined_rooms, /publicRooms, /members from one source over a short window — orders of magnitude above what a real Matrix client does. Rationale: Anchors on the actor's quoted boast — '~650,000 messages and information on over 73,000 accounts' from one account — which is only achievable through enumeration of the Matrix client-server API. The endpoint list comes from the Matrix spec's discovery/directory routes (sync, joined_rooms, publicRooms, members, directory). Bursty per-source counts + multi-shard touch is the article-specific differentiator: the actor explicitly noted they crossed shards from a single education-shard account.
ATT&CKT1213 T1087 T1087.003
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
let MatrixEnumPaths = dynamic(["/_matrix/client/r0/sync", "/_matrix/client/v3/sync", "/joined_rooms", "/publicRooms", "/members", "/directory/room", "/directory/list"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "tchap.gouv.fr"
| where RemoteUrl has_any (MatrixEnumPaths)
| extend Shard = tostring(parse_url(RemoteUrl).Host),
         Endpoint = tostring(parse_url(RemoteUrl).Path)
| summarize ApiCalls = count(),
            DistinctEndpoints = dcount(Endpoint),
            ShardsTouched = dcount(Shard),
            ShardList = make_set(Shard, 10),
            EndpointSample = make_set(Endpoint, 20),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where ApiCalls > 500 or DistinctEndpoints > 50 or ShardsTouched > 2  // 500/10min ≈ 50× a Matrix client's idle sync rate
| order by ApiCalls desc
let MatrixEnumPaths = dynamic(["/_matrix/client/r0/sync", "/_matrix/client/v3/sync", "/joined_rooms", "/publicRooms", "/members", "/directory/room", "/directory/list"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstHostname has "tchap.gouv.fr" or Url has "tchap.gouv.fr"
| where Url has_any (MatrixEnumPaths)
| extend Shard = tostring(parse_url(Url).Host),
         Endpoint = tostring(parse_url(Url).Path)
| summarize ApiCalls = count(),
            DistinctEndpoints = dcount(Endpoint),
            ShardsTouched = dcount(Shard),
            ShardList = make_set(Shard, 10),
            EndpointSample = make_set(Endpoint, 20),
            UserAgents = make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where ApiCalls > 500 or DistinctEndpoints > 50 or ShardsTouched > 2
| order by ApiCalls desc
(source:proxy OR source:windows.sysmon) (@http.host:(*tchap.gouv.fr OR *.tchap.gouv.fr) OR @http.url:*tchap.gouv.fr*) (@http.url_path:*/_matrix/client/*/sync* OR @http.url_path:*/_matrix/client/*/joined_rooms* OR @http.url_path:*/_matrix/client/*/publicRooms* OR @http.url_path:*/_matrix/client/*/members* OR @http.url_path:*/_matrix/client/*/directory/*)

New FROST Attack Lets Websites Track What Sites and Apps You Open via SSD Timing

The Hacker News
2026-06-09 7 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A malicious website can work out which sites you visit and which apps you open, using nothing but JavaScript and the timing of your SSD. The attack, called FROST, needs no native code, no extension, and no permission prompt. You open the page, leave the tab sitting there, and it watches the drive for contention in the background. Researchers at Graz University of Technology built it and

ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002 T1528 T1555.003 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Browser writing oversized OPFS file (potential FROST SSD-timing side-channel)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
[LLM] Browser writing oversized OPFS file (potential FROST SSD-timing side-channel) Reconnaissance Low
Hunts for a browser process (Chrome/Edge/Firefox/Safari) writing a file >4 GB into the per-origin Origin Private File System storage path. FROST requires an OPFS file larger than physical RAM so reads bypass the page cache and reach the SSD — legitimate OPFS use rarely exceeds a few hundred MB, so an unexplained multi-GB OPFS allocation is the only host-side tell the Graz paper offers. Rationale: Anchored on the only host-side artefact the article actually names: 'watching your browser's storage for an unexplained multi-gigabyte file is another tell.' The >4 GB threshold mirrors FROST's stated requirement (file > physical RAM to defeat the page cache). Browser-process scope + per-origin OPFS path roots (Chrome/Edge: 'File System/' inside the profile; Firefox: 'storage/default/...fs/'; Safari/WebKit: 'Library/Safari/Storage' or 'Library/WebKit') are taken from the standardised OPFS-on-disk locations referenced by the W3C spec the article cites. No external corroboration searched — there is no actor / malware family / CVE attached, and the IOCs extracted by the pipeline (malicious.app, victim.com, receiver.app, sender.app) are clearly academic placeholders from the paper, not real C2.
ATT&CKT1592.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","Google Chrome","firefox","Safari","com.apple.WebKit.Networking")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\File System\", "/File System/", "/storage/default/", ".mozilla/firefox", "/Library/Safari/Storage", "/Library/WebKit")
| where FileSize > 4000000000  // 4 GB — FROST requires file > physical RAM
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by FileSize desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome","msedge","firefox","brave","Safari","WebKit")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\File System\", "/File System/", "/storage/default/", ".mozilla/firefox", "/Library/Safari/Storage", "/Library/WebKit")
| where TargetFileSize > 4000000000
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize
| order by TargetFileSize desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

[LLM] Hades/Miasma PyPI poisoned package installation (26 named packages) Delivery High
Detects pip / python invoking installation of any of the 26 PyPI packages and versions Socket / StepSecurity identified in the Hades wave of the Miasma supply-chain campaign. Catches the very first foothold before the *-setup.pth hook runs on next interpreter start. Rationale: Uses the verbatim 26 package names from the article's two Hades clusters (the 19-package PyPI cluster + the 7-package bioinformatics cluster). Pip-install command line with these exact names is effectively zero-FP outside of incident-response activity.

[LLM] Python interpreter downloading Bun runtime ZIP from oven-sh GitHub release Installation High
Hades/Miasma stages a JavaScript stealer by having the malicious .pth or __init__.py hook download the standalone Bun runtime ZIP from github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases. Detecting Python/pip as the parent of that network connection is the cleanest cross-platform pivot — Bun is not a Python dependency in any normal supply chain. Rationale: Article: 'The compromised releases shipped a *-setup.pth file that attempts to execute automatically during Python startup, download the Bun JavaScript runtime, and run an obfuscated JavaScript payload named _index.js.' StepSecurity also notes Bun is downloaded as a standalone ZIP — pivoting on python→github.com/oven-sh/bun is the staging-link signature.
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.007
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python","python3","pip.exe","pip3.exe","bash","sh","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("github.com/oven-sh/bun","objects.githubusercontent.com")
   and (RemoteUrl has_any ("bun-linux","bun-windows","bun-darwin","/releases/download/") or RemoteUrl endswith ".zip")
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python","python3","pip.exe","pip3.exe")
       or FileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python","python3","pip.exe","pip3.exe")
    | project DeviceId, PyTimestamp = Timestamp, PyCmd = ProcessCommandLine
) on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (PyTimestamp .. PyTimestamp + 10m)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, PyCmd
| order by Timestamp desc
let BunUrlFrag = dynamic(["github.com/oven-sh/bun","objects.githubusercontent.com"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Url has_any (BunUrlFrag)
| where Url has_any ("bun-linux","bun-windows","bun-darwin","/releases/download/") or Url endswith ".zip"
| join kind=inner (
    ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","pip")
    | project DvcHostname, PyTime = TimeGenerated, PyCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine
) on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (PyTime .. PyTime + 10m)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, DstHostname, PyCmd
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Hades persistence: *-setup.pth file written into Python site-packages Installation High
The Hades cluster persists by dropping a `*-setup.pth` file into a site-packages directory. Python's `site` module executes any `import`/`exec` line in a `.pth` file at every interpreter start, so this file is the auto-run primitive. Detect creation of any file matching the pattern by a non-pip writer or with executable content inside. Rationale: Article: 'the use of a *-setup.pth file that's processed by Python's site module during interpreter startup, resulting in the execution of the malicious payload after installation.' The `-setup.pth` suffix in site-packages is unusual — legitimate .pth files are typically named after the package (e.g. easy-install.pth, distutils-precedence.pth), not '<pkg>-setup.pth'.
ATT&CKT1546 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith "-setup.pth"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\site-packages\", "/site-packages/", @"\dist-packages\", "/dist-packages/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName endswith "-setup.pth"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\site-packages\", "/site-packages/", @"\dist-packages\", "/dist-packages/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Hades PyPI Persistence via -setup.pth Python Startup Hook
id: 9b2c8d3e-1f4a-4b5c-8d6e-7a8b9c0d1e2f
description: Detects creation of a *-setup.pth file inside Python site-packages, the persistence primitive used by the Hades wave of the Miasma PyPI supply-chain campaign (June 2026). Python's site module auto-executes any import/exec line in a .pth file on every interpreter start.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/09

detection:

    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\site-packages\'
      - '/site-packages/'
      - '\dist-packages\'
      - '/dist-packages/'
  condition: selection
level: high

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\site-packages\*-setup.pth OR *\dist-packages\*-setup.pth) OR (source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:PATH @file.path:(*/site-packages/*-setup.pth OR */dist-packages/*-setup.pth))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/[\\\/](site|dist)-packages[\\\/].*-setup\.pth$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*-setup.pth" Filesystem.file_path IN ("*\\site-packages\\*","*/site-packages/*","*\\dist-packages\\*","*/dist-packages/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*-setup.pth" Filesystem.file_path IN ("*\\site-packages\\*","*/site-packages/*","*\\dist-packages\\*","*/dist-packages/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
[LLM] Bun runtime reading developer credential files (.npmrc / .pypirc / .ssh / .env / cloud configs) Actions on Objectives High
The Hades JavaScript stealer (_index.js) executes inside Bun and walks the developer's home directory for credentials: .npmrc, .pypirc, .env, .aws/credentials, .config/gcloud, .azure, .docker, ~/.ssh/, ~/.config/Claude, MCP configs, Vault tokens, shell histories. Bun touching those paths is the credential_access signature. Rationale: Article enumerates the exact target set: 'secrets associated with GitHub, npm, PyPI, RubyGems, JFrog, CircleCI, Anthropic, AWS, GCP, Azure, and Kubernetes, along with Docker configurations, Vault tokens, SSH keys, shell histories, .env files, .npmrc files, .pypirc files, Claude/MCP configurations.' Bun as the reader is what makes this fire — legitimate dev tools (git, gh, aws-cli) reading these is normal; Bun reading 3+ distinct credential paths in one session is not.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
let SecretPaths = pack_array(".npmrc",".pypirc",".env","credentials","id_rsa","id_ed25519","gcloud",".azure","config.json","mcp.json",".vault-token",".bash_history",".zsh_history","gh-token",".jfrog",".gem");
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")
| where ActionType in ("FileOpened","FileCreated","FileModified")
   and (FolderPath has_any (@"\.ssh\", "/.ssh/", @"\.aws\", "/.aws/", @"\.azure\", "/.azure/", @"\gcloud\", "/gcloud/", @"\.docker\", "/.docker/", @"\Claude\", "/Claude/", @"\.config\Claude\", @"\.jfrog\", "/.jfrog/")
        or FileName in~ (".npmrc",".pypirc",".env","credentials",".vault-token",".bash_history",".zsh_history","mcp.json")
        or FileName startswith "id_")
| summarize SecretReads = dcount(FolderPath), Paths = make_set(strcat(FolderPath, FileName), 50), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where SecretReads >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")
| where EventType in ("FileAccessed","FileOpened","FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/.ssh/", @"\.ssh\", "/.aws/", @"\.aws\", "/.azure/", @"\.azure\", "/gcloud/", "/.docker/", "/Claude/", "/.jfrog/")
    or TargetFileName in~ (".npmrc",".pypirc",".env","credentials",".vault-token",".bash_history",".zsh_history","mcp.json")
    or TargetFileName startswith "id_"
| summarize SecretReads = dcount(TargetFilePath), Paths = make_set(TargetFilePath, 50), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName
| where SecretReads >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc

[LLM] gh-token-monitor service install or rm -rf wiper command (Hades self-destruct) Actions on Objectives High
Hades installs a background service named 'gh-token-monitor' that doubles as a wiper — if the developer revokes the stolen GitHub token, the service triggers `rm -rf ~/; rm -rf ~/Documents`. Either the service-install or the wiper command is article-specific and warrants an alert. Rationale: Article: 'Install a background service named gh-token-monitor that acts as a wiper by removing all data (rm -rf ~/; rm -rf ~/Documents) if the stolen GitHub token is revoked by the developer.' The service name and the exact wiper command line are both unique enough to alert directly on string match.
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1543.002 T1485
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Services
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "gh-token-monitor"
     and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sc create","sc.exe create","systemctl","launchctl","New-Service","systemd")
  | extend Pivot = "service_install"
),
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)rm\s+-rf\s+(~/?|/home/[^/\s]+/?|/Users/[^/\s]+/?)\s*;\s*rm\s+-rf\s+~?/?Documents"
  | extend Pivot = "wiper"
),
( DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType == "ServiceInstalled"
  | where AdditionalFields has "gh-token-monitor" or FileName has "gh-token-monitor" or ProcessCommandLine has "gh-token-monitor"
  | extend Pivot = "service_event"
)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Pivot, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
( ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "gh-token-monitor"
     and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("sc create","sc.exe create","systemctl","launchctl","New-Service")
  | extend Pivot = "service_install"
),
( ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)rm\s+-rf\s+(~/?|/home/[^/\s]+/?|/Users/[^/\s]+/?)\s*;\s*rm\s+-rf\s+~?/?Documents"
  | extend Pivot = "wiper"
),
( SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where EventID == 7045
  | where ServiceName has "gh-token-monitor" or ServiceFileName has "gh-token-monitor"
  | extend Pivot = "service_event", ActingProcessCommandLine = ServiceFileName, DvcHostname = Computer, ActorUsername = SubjectUserName
)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, Pivot, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Hades Wiper Command or gh-token-monitor Service Install
id: 7c5b9e8a-2d3c-4f5b-9e7d-3a4b5c6d7e8a
description: Detects either installation of a service literally named 'gh-token-monitor' or execution of the Hades wiper command 'rm -rf ~/; rm -rf ~/Documents' attributed to the Hades / Miasma PyPI campaign.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/hades-pypi-attack-19-packages-poisoned.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/09
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.impact
  - attack.t1543.003
  - attack.t1485
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_service:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'gh-token-monitor'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'sc create'
      - 'sc.exe create'
      - 'systemctl'
      - 'launchctl'
      - 'New-Service'
  selection_wiper:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'rm -rf'
      - 'Documents'
    CommandLine|re: '(?i)rm\s+-rf\s+(~|/home/|/Users/).*;\s*rm\s+-rf\s+~?/?Documents'
  condition: selection_service or selection_wiper
level: critical

(source:windows.sysmon OR source:windows.security OR source:linux.auditd) AND ((@CommandLine:(*gh-token-monitor*) AND @CommandLine:(*sc?create* OR *systemctl* OR *launchctl* OR *New-Service*)) OR (@process.command_line:(*gh-token-monitor*) AND @process.command_line:(*systemctl* OR *launchctl* OR *sc?create*)) OR @CommandLine:("rm -rf ~/*; rm -rf ~/Documents" OR "rm -rf ~; rm -rf ~/Documents") OR @process.command_line:("rm -rf ~/*; rm -rf ~/Documents" OR "rm -rf ~; rm -rf ~/Documents"))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (CommandLine=/gh-token-monitor/i AND CommandLine=/(sc\s+create|systemctl|launchctl|New-Service)/i) OR CommandLine=/rm\s+-rf\s+(~\/?|\/home\/[^\/\s]+|\/Users\/[^\/\s]+)\s*;\s*rm\s+-rf\s+~?\/?Documents/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
(`endpoint_processes` OR `linux_processes`)
| eval is_service_install=if(match(process,"(?i)gh-token-monitor") AND (match(process,"(?i)(sc\\.exe|sc\\s+create|systemctl|launchctl|new-service)")),1,0),
       is_wiper=if(match(process,"(?i)rm\\s+-rf\\s+(~/?|/Users/[^/]+|/home/[^/]+)\\s*;\\s*rm\\s+-rf\\s+~?/Documents") OR match(process,"(?i)rm\\s+-rf\\s+~/?\\s*;?\\s*rm\\s+-rf\\s+~/Documents"),1,0)
| where is_service_install=1 OR is_wiper=1
| stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(process) as commands by host user parent_process_name process_name is_service_install is_wiper
[LLM] Hades C2: GitHub commit search for campaign markers TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime / firedalazer Command & Control High
Hades retrieves staged payloads by polling the GitHub commits API for two unique marker strings: 'TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime' (Base64 JS payload) and 'firedalazer' (Python dropper). Either string appearing in process command lines, HTTP requests, or DNS/URL telemetry on a dev host is a high-fidelity C2 indicator. Rationale: Article: 'the malware queries GitHub commits for the keyword TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime to extract a Base64-encoded string containing a JavaScript payload. It also polls GitHub for commits matching the keyword firedalazer so as to fetch a Python-based dropper.' Both strings are sufficiently unique (random-looking concatenations) that any appearance in process/web/DNS telemetry is essentially zero-FP outside of threat-hunting activity.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Web.Web
let Markers = dynamic(["TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime","firedalazer"]);
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (Markers)
  | extend Pivot = "process", Url = ""
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Pivot, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, Url
),
( DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteUrl has_any (Markers)
  | extend Pivot = "network", FileName = InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Pivot, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, Url = RemoteUrl
)
| order by Timestamp desc
let Markers = dynamic(["TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime","firedalazer"]);
union isfuzzy=true
( ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (Markers)
  | extend Pivot = "process", Url = ""
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, Pivot, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Url
),
( ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Url has_any (Markers)
  | extend Pivot = "web", ActingProcessName = "", ActingProcessCommandLine = "", ActorUsername = SrcUsername
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname = SrcHostname, ActorUsername, Pivot, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Url
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Hades Campaign GitHub C2 Marker Strings
id: 5a6b7c8d-9e0f-1a2b-3c4d-5e6f7a8b9c0d
description: Detects either of the two Hades / Miasma GitHub commit-marker strings (TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime, firedalazer) appearing in a process command line — the malware searches GitHub for these to retrieve Base64-encoded JS payload and the Python dropper respectively.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/hades-pypi-attack-19-packages-poisoned.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/09
tags:

  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1102.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime'
      - 'firedalazer'
  condition: selection
level: high

(@CommandLine:(*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime* OR *firedalazer*) OR @process.command_line:(*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime* OR *firedalazer*) OR @http.url:(*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime* OR *firedalazer*) OR @http.url_details.queryString:(*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime* OR *firedalazer*) OR @DestinationHostname:(*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime* OR *firedalazer*))
(#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/(TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime|firedalazer)/i) OR (#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime|firedalazer)/i) OR (#event_simpleName=ScriptControlScanInfo ScriptContent=/(TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime|firedalazer)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, #event_simpleName], function=count())
NETWORK
